questions.question: The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. What does a minimum-weight perfect matching of these vertices choose?
options: Pairs such that every odd vertex is in exactly one pair, with the smallest total pair cost
Pairs such that every odd vertex is in at least one pair, with the smallest total pair cost
For every odd vertex, its nearest other odd vertex, taken as its partner in a pair
One pair for each edge of the network, with the two endpoints of that edge as partners

questions.question: Two odd-degree vertices $A$ and $C$ of a network are joined by a direct edge of length 7, and there is also a route $A$–$E$–$C$ with edge lengths 2 and 3. No shorter route exists. Which pair cost $d_{AC}$ is used when pairing odd vertices?
options: $d_{AC}=7$, the length of the direct edge
$d_{AC}=2$, the number of edges on it
$d_{AC}=5$, the shortest-path distance
$d_{AC}=12$, the total of both routes

questions.question: In any finite undirected network, the odd-degree vertices are to be split into pairs. Why is such a pairing always possible?
options: Degrees sum to twice the edge count, so the odd vertices are even in number.
Every network has exactly four vertices of odd degree, which split into two pairs.
A connected network lets any two odd vertices be paired along some path.
Odd vertices always come in adjacent couples joined by an edge of the network.

questions.question: The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. Why can the cheapest pairing not be found by repeatedly taking the cheapest remaining pair?
options: The cheapest pair is always in the optimum, so repeating the step is optimal.
A locally cheap pair may leave expensive pairs for the remaining vertices.
The order of choosing pairs does not matter, as all pairings cost the same.
Repeating the step works for four vertices but fails for six or more.

questions.question: The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. Which restriction on the partners does the pairing problem impose?
options: None: any odd vertex may be paired with any other odd vertex of the network.
Partners must come from two fixed groups, one vertex from each group.
Partners must be adjacent, joined directly by an edge of the network.
Partners must alternate around the network, each next to the following.

questions.question: A network has exactly four odd-degree vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, which are to be split into two pairs. How many different complete pairings are there to compare?
Four odd-degree vertices have shortest-path distances $d_{AB}=3$, $d_{AC}=5$, $d_{AD}=4$, $d_{BC}=4$, $d_{BD}=6$, $d_{CD}=2$. What is the cost of a minimum-weight perfect matching?

Odd vertices $A$, $B$, $D$, $E$ are paired with binary variables $x_{ij}$ for $i<j$ in alphabetical order, where $x_{ij}=1$ means $i$ and $j$ form a pair. Which constraint says that $B$ is in exactly one pair?
options: $x_{AB}+x_{BD}+x_{BE}\le 1$

questions.question: Four odd vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are paired with a binary variable $x_{ij}$ for each unordered pair $i<j$, where $x_{ij}=1$ means $i$ and $j$ form a pair. How many binary variables does the model have?
options: 12 variables, one for each ordered pair
3 variables, one for each pairing
6 variables, one per unordered pair
4 variables, one for each vertex

questions.question: Odd vertices $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ have pair costs $d_{PQ}=2$, $d_{PR}=6$, $d_{PS}=3$, $d_{QR}=4$, $d_{QS}=5$, $d_{RS}=7$. The binary pairing variables are $x_{PS}=x_{QR}=1$ and all others 0. What is the value of the objective $\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}x_{ij}$?

The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. The model has binary variables $x_{ij}$ only for $i<j$. What is the reason?
options: Pairs may only be linked from the smaller to the larger index.
Pairs with $i>j$ are forbidden, which makes some pairs impossible.
Shortest paths from $i$ to $j$ may differ from those from $j$ to $i$.
A pair is unordered; one variable per pair avoids counting it twice.

questions.question: The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. The binary model requires, for each odd vertex, that the variables of the pairs containing it sum to exactly 1. What happens if '$=1$' is replaced by '$\le 1$'?
options: Nothing changes, since a cheapest solution pairs everyone anyway.
Setting every variable to zero becomes feasible and pairs nobody.
The model becomes infeasible, as no pairing satisfies it.
Only the binary requirement matters, so the change is harmless.

questions.question: When the odd-degree vertices of a network are paired and each pair is to be linked by a route in the network, why is the pair cost $d_{ij}$ taken to be the shortest-path distance between $i$ and $j$?
options: Pairs must be joined by a direct edge, so $d_{ij}$ is the edge length.
Any route may link the pair, and the cheapest route has that length.
The cost should count edges, so the route with fewest edges is used.
The average length of all routes is used to treat every route fairly.

questions.question: Odd vertices $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ have pair costs $d_{PQ}=1$, $d_{RS}=10$, $d_{PR}=4$, $d_{QS}=4$, $d_{PS}=5$, $d_{QR}=5$. A planner first takes the cheapest pair, then pairs the rest. What does the planner pay, and what is the minimum?
options: Planner 11, minimum 11
Planner 10, minimum 8
Planner 8, minimum 8
Planner 11, minimum 8

questions.question: A network has edges $A$–$B$ 3, $B$–$C$ 2, $C$–$D$ 9, $D$–$A$ 5, $A$–$E$ 1, $B$–$E$ 6, $C$–$E$ 1, $D$–$E$ 1; its odd-degree vertices are $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$. Pair costs are shortest-path distances. What is the cost of a minimum-weight perfect matching?
Six odd-degree vertices $A$ to $F$ of a network must be grouped into three disjoint pairs. In how many distinct ways can this be done?

Odd vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ have pair costs $d_{AB}=d_{AC}=d_{AD}=1$ and $d_{BC}=d_{BD}=d_{CD}=10$; binary $x_{ij}$ ($i<j$) equals 1 when $i$ and $j$ are paired. If each vertex constraint read '$\ge 1$' instead of '$=1$', what would the minimum of $\sum d_{ij}x_{ij}$ be?
options: 11, the same as with equality constraints
No solution, since no pairing satisfies it
3, with vertex $A$ in three pairs
2, with the pairs AB and AC only

questions.question: The odd-degree vertices of a network are to be paired; the cost $d_{ij}$ of pairing $i$ and $j$ is their shortest-path distance. For each odd vertex $i$, let $m_i$ be the distance to its nearest other odd vertex, and let $L$ be half the sum of all $m_i$. How does $L$ relate to the minimum pairing cost?
options: $L$ never exceeds the minimum cost, but it can fall strictly below it.
$L$ always equals the minimum cost, as each vertex pairs with its nearest.
$L$ can exceed the minimum cost, since nearest distances are counted twice.
$L$ equals the cost of pairing the cheapest pair first, then repeating.

questions.question: Six odd vertices split into clusters {A, $B$, C} and {D, $E$, F}: pair costs are 1 within a cluster and 10 between clusters. The binary pairing model (exactly one pair per vertex) is relaxed to $0\le x_{ij}\le1$. What are the relaxed optimum and the cheapest true pairing?
options: Relaxed 3, pairing 12
Relaxed 3, pairing 3
Relaxed 6, pairing 12
Relaxed 12, pairing 12

questions.question: Odd vertices $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ have pair costs $d_{PQ}=6$, $d_{RS}=5$, $d_{PR}=3$, $d_{QS}=4$, $d_{PS}=5$, $d_{QR}=6$, so PR with QS (7) is the cheapest pairing. Below which value must $d_{PQ}$ fall for PQ with RS to become strictly cheaper?
options: Below 3
Below 6
Below 2
Below 7
